Linas

Thanks for the leading question. My guess is how well it describes the data. Since model is given (PBPK) we just want to estimate parameters well. Based on the book of P. Bonate on PKPD modeling & simulation they like tight fit. PBPK is a mechanistic model and as such has bias. I still have to comprehend the concept of quality of population model but maybe I can find some clues in this list.

messages.author: f2961c15f7afbca6
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] goodness of fit of PK hierarchical stan models
parts:
Linus,

traditional goodness-of-fit diagnostics in PK-realm don't necessarily translate well to PBPK, as the model simplifications implicit with compartmental models allow for more reasonable mapping of parameters to data. Eg, given a one compartment model with CL/V and concentration data, doing a visual or posterior predictive check can help easily identify where model misspecification arises, and the parameter the maps to that portion of the data (eg. trough concentrations missed = problems with CL or compartmental structure)

Likewise CWRES-vs-IDV type plots and DV vs IPRED diagnostics are also similarly used, but don't map well to the multitude of PBPK params.

My advice is, as with simpler models, identify the key questions the model is trying to address, and most importantly use quality science and mechanistic knowledge to drive the model construction. Then supplement with diagnostic plots that adequately show that such a model is not unduly biased to address those questions. For example, given a therapeutic window of 10 ng/mL efficacy cutpoint, given a PPC that shows that at the 10th 50th and 90th percentiles, the observed and fit data are aligned, gives confidence that your model can suitably address the question at hand, even if, say, the peak concentrations are slightly off. 

Sensitivity analysis of the param values, and leveraging prior literature to inform your priors, and some basic diagnostics similar to those mentioned above should be sufficient I would think. 

Here are some helpful links

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2751255/
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4761232/

messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] goodness of fit of PK hierarchical stan models
parts:
Devin,

Thanks a lot. It seems that 0.5 quantiles and 95% credible intervals show good alignment with the data. As you have suggested some of parameters such as volume, flow rates, kpus are taken from the literature (I am working on ACAT model which translates to 34 states since the drug is highly solvable). I am right now estimating kidney and ATAT Vmax & Km in addition to the scaling factor to kpus). I have bunch of patients (19) so use hierarchical model and visually comparing fits each patient I feel is not enough. Thus I would like to have some formal assessments as in a https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3276744/. The papers you have mentioned I assume will provide a good insight as well. Essentially I want to justify that model is good enough without going into estimation of gastric residence time or expression levels. Another goal is to assess which error model - additive or additive+proportional is better suited. Intuition tells that additive+proportional should make more sense but maybe just additive is enough since there is modeling error anyway. One parameter in a 2 day simulation may chop off some time.

Linas

Linus,

You'd just do a simple residuals. The conditional weighting was due to the approximation of the likelihood via first order method transformations - given STAN does not need to use such an approximation, the residuals themselves should be sufficient to evaluate.
